1.title: Geographically Weighted Regression: A Method for Exploring Spatial Nonstationarity
1.abstract: Geographically weighted regression is a method for exploring spatial nonstationarity. It allows for the analysis of spatial variation in relationships across geographic space, offering insights into how relationships may differ across locations.
author: author-1
author-2

reference_mentions: Various spatial prediction models [21] and spatial data analysis tools [24] have been developed to support geographic analysis. In this work, we focus on two local spatial models widely used in spatial analysis: Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) [1], and its recent extension, Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) [2]. GWR extends the classical linear regression model [20] by capturing spatial heterogeneity with influence spreading over the space in a constant scale. MGWR further improves GWR models where local influences are modeled in different spatial windows.

2.title: Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR)
2.abstract: Geographically weighted regression (GWR) is a popular approach for spatially varying relationships. However, GWR is limited by its reliance on the assumption that the spatial relationships can be adequately captured by local linear models. In this paper, we introduce multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR), which overcomes this limitation by allowing for varying relationships at multiple scales. MGWR incorporates a multiscale approach to address the inadequacies of single-scale modeling frameworks, offering more flexible model specifications for spatial data. We demonstrate the utility of MGWR using a case study of urban house prices, illustrating how it can reveal spatially varying influences that would be concealed when using GWR or traditional regression approaches.

3.title: NewsViews: an automated pipeline for creating custom geovisualizations for news
3.abstract: News media today face the challenge of effectively communicating complex data stories to their audiences. As data-driven decision-making becomes increasingly important, understanding how to represent and convey data in news articles is crucial. In this paper, we introduce NewsViews, an automated pipeline that generates custom geovisualizations from news articles. We describe the process by which we extract data from articles and create visualizations, as well as the technical and design challenges we encountered along the way. Our work contributes to the growing field of data journalism by providing tools that enhance the integration of data visualizations in storytelling.

4.title: Visualizing Multiple Variables Across Scale and Geography
4.abstract: This paper presents a framework for visualizing multiple variables across various scales and geographical contexts. We discuss the challenges and solutions for integrating data visualization techniques in the context of complex, multidimensional datasets.
author: author-11
author-12
author-13
author-14
reference_mentions: Most closely related to our work are the techniques that explain models from feature-level observation. Muhlbacher and ¨ Piringer [14] facilitated feature selection and optimization in regression models by partitioning the feature space into disjoint regions for visualization. Sedlmair et al. [17] proposed an abstract conceptual framework to discuss the visual parameter space analysis problems independent of the application domain. Goodwin et al. [4] extended visual parameter space analysis to the spatial domain, enabling the exploration of correlations between multiple variables that vary geographically at different spatial scales. While these techniques focus on explanations for domain experts, our work is designed to support explanations to experts and support their use of external information to contextualize these relationships and communicate their findings to a general audience. Our choice of text templates, as opposed to large language models, for narrative generation is to support control for reliability and reproducibility. All text generated must have a verifiable source and the generation of text for the analysis should always return the same results to ensure that the resulting analyses are not subject to misinformation.

5.title: Visualization Rhetoric: Framing Effects in Narrative Visualization
5.abstract: In this paper we investigate the rhetorical dimensions of narrative visualization. We characterize the storytelling techniques in data-driven documents through a specialized framing lens. We explore the visual language of narrative visualization and its influence on audience perception. We present an empirical study to evaluate how different presentational aspects affect viewer interpretations of data. Our findings illustrate the importance of visual framing in guiding viewer comprehension and the potential for narrative visualization to shape interpretation.

reference_mentions: Support for a variety of spatial models is integrated into the most widely used geographic information systems (GIS). However, these systems and notebooks do not support integrated external knowledge sources to help contextualize models [6]. They also require analysts to judiciously choose the proper tools at every stage of the analytical pipeline to build a well-trained model. This process necessitates a solid foundation in geographical concepts and can be time-consuming, even for seasoned analysts. Our goal is to enhance the spatial modeling process through a deliberately designed userfriendly workflow and automatically generated explanatory narratives guided by domain experts to promote the understanding of local contextual information from models. Our work focuses on improving model explainability, enabling interactive report authoring, and supporting contextualization through narrative generation. This is important in local models such as GWR and MGWR because the main output from such models is a set of local parameter estimates from each process being modeled, and the spatial variation in these estimates needs to be explained in terms of the contextualized environment of each location by providing additional contextual information for users.

7.abstract: Storytelling is becoming important in visualization. It motivates the researcher to take a break from technicalities and get back to the story of the data. Storytelling in visualizations helps us engage the audience, explain the context and uncover the meaning behind the data.

8.title: Interacting with Predictions: Visual Inspection of Black-box Machine Learning Models
8.abstract: This paper presents an approach to enable users to interactively inspect machine learning model predictions in order to better understand and trust these models. We detail our design of interactive visualizations and a novel method for providing explanations for predictions, and highlight how our approach enhances user trust through understanding.

reference_mentions: Narrative visualization is directly related to the concept of explainability, where the visualization authors seek to couple images and text to explain an underlying data analysis. With respect to model explainability, the visual analytics community has developed a variety of systems to support the interactive explanation of machine learning models (e.g. [22, 12]). Several model-independent approaches, e.g. EnsembleMatrix [25] and RuleMatrix [13], focus on the classifier's input-output behaviors to provide insight into the model classification results. EnsembleMatrix provides a visual summary of the model outputs, RuleMatrix uses a matrix-based visualization to explain classification results, and Prospector [8] explores the relationship between feature values and predictions by using partial dependence diagnostics.

14.title: A Partition-Based Framework for Building and Validating Regression Models
14.abstract: We present a partition-based framework for building and validating regression models. The proposed framework allows users to analyze regression models by separating the data space into distinct regions. Each segment’s characteristics can be summarized using interpretable regression models. We illustrate the applicability of our approach in various use cases, and we demonstrate that it enhances the interpretability of data analysis results.

reference_mentions: Most closely related to our work are the techniques that explain models from feature-level observation. Muhlbacher and ¨ Piringer [14] facilitated feature selection and optimization in regression models by partitioning the feature space into disjoint regions for visualization. Sedlmair et al. [17] proposed an abstract conceptual framework to discuss the visual parameter space analysis problems independent of the application domain. Goodwin et al. [4] extended visual parameter space analysis to the spatial domain, enabling the exploration of correlations between multiple variables that vary geographically at different spatial scales. While these techniques focus on explanations for domain experts, our work is designed to support explanations to experts and support their use of external information to contextualize these relationships and communicate their findings to a general audience. Our choice of text templates, as opposed to large language models, for narrative generation is to support control for reliability and reproducibility. All text generated must have a verifiable source and the generation of text for the analysis should always return the same results to ensure that the resulting analyses are not subject to misinformation.

25.title: EnsembleMatrix: interactive visualization to support machine learning with multiple classifiers
25.abstract: We present EnsembleMatrix, an interactive visualization tool that allows users to analyze and compare the performance of multiple classifiers. EnsembleMatrix integrates the traditional performance metrics with the visual representation of the classifiers' decision boundaries and feature importance, facilitating the machine learning workflow. We demonstrate EnsembleMatrix's effectiveness through a case study involving several classification tasks, revealing insights that are often overlooked by conventional methods.

reference_mentions: Narrative visualization is directly related to the concept of explainability, where the visualization authors seek to couple images and text to explain an underlying data analysis. With respect to model explainability, the visual analytics community has developed a variety of systems to support the interactive explanation of machine learning models (e.g. [22, 12]). Several model-independent approaches, e.g. EnsembleMatrix [25] and RuleMatrix [13], focus on the classifier's input-output behaviors to provide insight into the model classification results. EnsembleMatrix provides a visual summary of the model outputs, RuleMatrix uses a matrix-based visualization to explain classification results, and Prospector [8] explores the relationship between feature values and predictions by using partial dependence diagnostics.
